title: Predictive coding, Bayesian brain, and the free-energy idea
text:
13_03  PREDICTIVE CODING, THE BAYESIAN BRAIN, AND THE FREE-ENERGY IDEA

The previous sections asked how neurons carry and transform signals. This section asks a different, more ambitious question: what is the brain trying to compute? A family of theories answers that the brain is fundamentally an inference machine. It never sees the world directly, only noisy, ambiguous sensory data, and it must infer the hidden causes of those data, using prior knowledge, and act accordingly. These theories are the place where neuroscience and probabilistic machine learning are almost indistinguishable, and they are also the place where the most care is needed, because some versions are precise and testable while others are so general that critics have questioned whether they can be falsified.

HELMHOLTZ AND UNCONSCIOUS INFERENCE

Hermann von Helmholtz, whom we met measuring nerve conduction velocity in Chapter 2, argued in his work on physiological optics in the nineteenth century that perception involves "unconscious inference": the brain interprets sensations by drawing conclusions about their most likely causes, based on experience. Visual illusions are then not malfunctions but the results of reasonable inferences applied in unusual conditions. A shaded disc looks convex or concave depending on whether we assume light comes from above, an assumption that is usually right.

BAYES' RULE AS A MODEL OF PERCEPTION

The modern form of Helmholtz's idea uses Bayes' rule. Let s be a hidden state of the world (say, the true position of an object) and x the sensory data. Then

  P(s | x) = P(x | s) P(s) / P(x)

The likelihood P(x | s) describes how data are generated from the world, including noise. The prior P(s) describes what states are probable before seeing the data. The posterior P(s | x) combines them.

A worked example makes this concrete. Suppose you estimate an object's size from vision and touch, each giving a Gaussian estimate: vision says x_V with variance sigma_V^2, touch says x_H with variance sigma_H^2. With a flat prior, the optimal combined estimate is a weighted average

  s_hat = w_V x_V + w_H x_H,  with  w_V = (1/sigma_V^2) / (1/sigma_V^2 + 1/sigma_H^2)

and w_H = 1 - w_V. Each cue is weighted by its reliability (inverse variance), and the combined variance

  sigma^2 = 1 / (1/sigma_V^2 + 1/sigma_H^2)

is smaller than either alone. Marc Ernst and Martin Banks reported in Nature in 2002 that human observers combining visual and haptic size information behaved close to this optimal rule: when the experimenters degraded the visual stimulus with noise, observers relied more on touch, by about the amount predicted. Anyone who has built a sensor-fusion system will recognise this as the measurement update of a Kalman filter. Indeed the Kalman filter is exactly recursive Bayesian inference for linear Gaussian systems, and many models of motor control and sensorimotor learning (for example by Daniel Wolpert and colleagues) use it as a model of how the brain tracks the state of the body.

Priors explain biases. Yair Weiss, Eero Simoncelli and Edward Adelson reported in Nature Neuroscience in 2002 that a Bayesian observer with a prior favouring slow speeds accounts for a range of motion illusions, including the perception that low-contrast stimuli move more slowly: when the data are weak (low contrast, broad likelihood), the prior pulls the estimate toward slow speeds. Alan Stocker and Simoncelli later showed in 2006 how priors and likelihoods can be estimated from human psychophysics.

How might neurons represent probability distributions? Proposals include probabilistic population codes, in which the pattern of Poisson-like spike counts across a population encodes a whole likelihood function, as described in 13_01 (Ma, Beck, Latham and Pouget, 2006); sampling-based codes, in which activity over time represents samples from the posterior; and codes in which neurons represent log probabilities. Which, if any, the brain uses is unresolved.

PREDICTIVE CODING

Predictive coding is a specific hypothesis about how the brain could implement inference with hierarchical feedback. Its roots are in signal processing. In television and telephone engineering in the 1950s, predictive coding meant transmitting only the difference between a signal and its prediction from previous values, which saves bandwidth because natural signals are highly predictable. Mandyam Srinivasan, Simon Laughlin and Andreas Dubs proposed in 1982 that the centre-surround receptive fields of the retina (Chapter 8) perform a similar operation: the surround predicts the centre from neighbouring pixels, and the cell transmits the residual, removing spatial redundancy in natural images.

Rajesh Rao and Dana Ballard proposed in Nature Neuroscience in 1999 a hierarchical version for visual cortex. Each level of the hierarchy holds an estimate of the causes of its input, r. It sends a prediction down to the level below through feedback connections, and the level below sends back only the prediction error. In equations for one level with input x, generative weights U and estimate r:

  prediction:        x_hat = f(U r)
  error:             e = x - f(U r)
  inference update:  dr/dt proportional to U^T e - (prior term on r)
  learning:          dU proportional to e r^T

The estimate r is adjusted to reduce prediction error (inference), and the weights U are adjusted Hebbian-style, as products of error and activity, to improve predictions over time (learning). Both steps are gradient descent on a sum of squared errors, which is the negative log probability of a Gaussian generative model. Rao and Ballard showed that such a network trained on natural images learned receptive fields similar to simple cells, and that it explained "extra-classical" receptive field effects such as end-stopping: a neuron responds less to a long line than a short one because the long line is predicted by higher levels, leaving less error.

The theory makes a structural prediction: there should be two functionally distinct populations, representation units and error units, with feedforward connections carrying errors and feedback carrying predictions. Andre Bastos, Karl Friston and colleagues in 2012 proposed how this could map onto the layers of the canonical cortical microcircuit, with superficial pyramidal cells sending errors forward and deep pyramidal cells sending predictions back.

EVIDENCE

Several lines of evidence are consistent with predictive processing.

Repetition suppression and mismatch responses. Neural responses decrease for repeated or expected stimuli and increase for unexpected ones. In human EEG, the mismatch negativity, a response to an oddball sound in a sequence, described by Risto Naatanen and colleagues in 1978, has been interpreted as a prediction error, though other explanations such as adaptation also contribute.

Sensorimotor prediction in mouse cortex. Georg Keller, Tobias Bonhoeffer and Mark Hubener reported in 2012 that neurons in mouse visual cortex responded strongly when the visual flow that normally accompanies running was unexpectedly halted, a mismatch between predicted and actual feedback. Subsequent work by Keller's group and others examined specific cell types and layers carrying such signals.

Expectation in cortex. Studies in humans and monkeys found that expected stimuli can evoke weaker but more sharply tuned responses, consistent with suppression of predictable components.

The evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Many observations predicted by predictive coding are also predicted by other mechanisms, such as adaptation or attention, and clean evidence for separate error and prediction populations is still debated. Reviews by researchers sympathetic to the theory and by critics both emphasise that predictive coding is a family of models with different specific predictions.

THE FREE-ENERGY PRINCIPLE

Karl Friston, a neuroimaging researcher at University College London known for developing statistical parametric mapping for fMRI analysis (Chapter 10), proposed in the 2000s a broader framework called the free-energy principle, summarised in a 2010 review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience. Its core mathematical idea comes from variational inference in statistics and machine learning.

Exact Bayesian inference requires the posterior P(s | x), which is usually intractable. Instead, choose an approximate distribution q(s) and minimise the variational free energy

  F = E_q[ log q(s) - log P(x, s) ]
    = KL( q(s) || P(s | x) ) - log P(x)

Because the KL divergence is non-negative, F is an upper bound on surprise, -log P(x). Minimising F with respect to q makes q approximate the true posterior (perception); minimising it with respect to model parameters improves the generative model (learning). Under Gaussian assumptions, minimising F reduces to minimising precision-weighted prediction errors, which recovers predictive coding.

Friston added that agents can also reduce surprise by acting to make their sensations match predictions, a scheme called active inference. Moving your eyes to where you expect to see something, or a reflex arc restoring a predicted posture, can be cast as action that minimises prediction error. Friston extended the principle to claim that any self-organising system that maintains itself in a bounded set of states (as living things must) can be described as minimising free energy.

The principle has been influential and contested. Supporters value it as a unifying framework connecting perception, action, learning and attention (attention as estimating the precision of prediction errors). Critics argue that in its most general form it is closer to a mathematical framework than an empirical theory: almost any behaviour can be described as minimising free energy under some generative model, so it is hard to falsify without specifying that model. Specific process theories derived from it, however, make testable predictions. A fair summary is that variational inference is a precise and powerful idea, predictive coding is one testable algorithmic proposal, and the broader free-energy principle is a framework whose empirical content depends on the specific models built from it.

CONNECTIONS TO AI AND MACHINE LEARNING

1. The same mathematics. The variational free energy is exactly the negative of the evidence lower bound (ELBO) maximised when training variational autoencoders, introduced by Diederik Kingma and Max Welling in 2013 and independently by Danilo Rezende, Shakir Mohamed and Daan Wierstra in 2014. An earlier ancestor, the Helmholtz machine of Peter Dayan, Geoffrey Hinton, Radford Neal and Richard Zemel (1995), was named after Helmholtz's unconscious inference and paired a recognition network with a generative network, trained by the wake-sleep algorithm. A VAE's encoder is the q(s) of the free-energy principle; its decoder is the generative model P(x | s).

2. Prediction as the training signal. The most successful AI systems of recent years are trained to predict. Large language models minimise the cross-entropy of next-token prediction, which is the average surprise -log P(x). Self-supervised vision models predict masked image patches or representations of one view from another. This is not evidence that they implement predictive coding as Rao and Ballard described it, since they are trained with backpropagation and usually lack explicit error units. But it shows the power of the idea that learning to predict sensory input builds useful internal models. Video prediction networks such as PredNet, by William Lotter, Gabriel Kreiman and David Cox (2016), were directly inspired by predictive coding and were reported to reproduce some neural and perceptual phenomena.

3. Predictive coding approximates backpropagation. James Whittington and Rafal Bogacz showed in 2017 that predictive coding networks, with only local Hebbian-like updates, can approximate the weight updates of backpropagation under certain conditions. Later work by Beren Millidge and colleagues extended this to arbitrary computation graphs. This is one of the most interesting results bearing on the Hebb-versus-backprop question of Chapter 7: local prediction-error learning in a hierarchical network can, in principle, approximate global gradient descent.

4. World models and model-based RL. Active inference's emphasis on generative models used for planning parallels model-based reinforcement learning and "world models" (for example by David Ha and Jurgen Schmidhuber in 2018, and the Dreamer agents by Danijar Hafner and colleagues), which learn latent dynamics models and plan or train policies in imagination.

5. Calibrated uncertainty. The Bayesian brain emphasises representing uncertainty, not just point estimates. Standard deep networks are often overconfident. Bayesian deep learning, ensembles and calibration methods try to give machines the reliability-weighting humans show in cue combination.

SUMMARY

The Bayesian brain hypothesis, descended from Helmholtz, treats perception as inference that combines likelihoods and priors, and human cue combination often matches optimal predictions. Predictive coding proposes a neural implementation in which feedback carries predictions and feedforward carries errors, with suggestive but not decisive evidence. The free-energy principle generalises this to variational inference and action, and is best treated as a framework whose testable content lies in specific models. The mathematics is shared with variational autoencoders, self-supervised prediction and model-based reinforcement learning, making this one of the closest meeting points of neuroscience and AI.
